title: The Tabernacle Tent, Its Frames, and the Veil
summary: God describes the tabernacle's structure: an inner layer of ten linen curtains woven with cherubim, a tent of eleven goat-hair curtains over it, and outer coverings of red-dyed ram skins and fine leather. The walls are gold-covered acacia frames set in silver bases and braced with crossbars. A veil woven with cherubim divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where the ark stands, and an embroidered screen closes the entrance.
story: Chapter 25 described the furniture at the heart of the sanctuary; chapter 26 builds the house around it. At the end of the chapter God puts each piece in its room: the ark behind the veil, the table on the north side, the lampstand on the south. The structure will be made in chapter 36 and set up in chapter 40, where the cloud will cover it and the glory fill it. The veil introduced here becomes one of the most important boundaries in Scripture, the line that only the high priest may cross, once a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).
historical:
As described, the tabernacle was a rectangular tent about 30 cubits long and 10 wide (roughly 45 by 15 feet, or 14 by 4.5 meters), divided into a Holy Place and a Most Holy Place. Reconstructions differ, because the text gives instructions for craftsmen rather than a complete blueprint: the form of the frames, the way the curtains draped, and whether the tent had a ridge or a flat top are all debated. Most reconstructions make the Most Holy Place a cube of ten cubits, matching the pattern of Solomon's temple, whose inner sanctuary was “twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high” (1 Kings 6:20).

The nearest ancient analogies are portable shrines and royal tents. Egyptian reliefs of Ramesses II's campaign against Kadesh in the thirteenth century BC show the king's tent within a rectangular camp, with the throne room at the rear, and scholars have noted its likeness to the tabernacle's layout and orientation. Collapsible frames overlaid with gold and joined with tenons and sockets are known from Egypt as well, the best example being the gilded canopy frame of Queen Hetepheres, mother of Khufu, found in her tomb at Giza.
cultural:
Goat-hair cloth was the ordinary material of nomads' tents in the Near East: dark, coarse, and waterproof, and Bedouin tents are still woven from it. From the outside, then, the tabernacle was a plain tent among tents, covered with ram skins and leather; its splendor was inside, seen only by the priests. The colors of the inner linen and the veil, blue, purple, and scarlet, were royal colors, and the cherubim woven into them marked the space as a heavenly King's throne room, guarded like the way to the tree of life after Eden (Genesis 3:24).

The metals follow the gradation of holiness: bronze for the bases of the entrance posts, silver for the bases of the frames, and gold for the frames and everything within. A priest going inward passed from bronze to silver to gold. The entrance faced east and the Most Holy Place lay to the west, so a worshiper approaching God faced west with the rising sun behind him. Some interpreters see a deliberate contrast with sun worship; Ezekiel later condemns men who turned their backs on the temple and were “bowing to the east in worship of the sun” (Ezekiel 8:16).
literary: The chapter is technical prose, dense with numbers, and its logic is spatial. It begins with the linen curtains that form the inner space (verses 1-6), adds the layers over them (verses 7-14), raises the frames that hold everything up (verses 15-30), and ends with the veil and screen that divide and close the tent (verses 31-37). Verse 30 repeats the refrain of 25:9 and 25:40 that all must follow the pattern shown on the mountain. The clasps are to join the curtains so that the tabernacle will be “a unit” (verse 6), one whole. The Hebrew idiom for joining one curtain to another is literally a woman to her sister, the ordinary way Hebrew says one to another, used here of curtains and frames.

outline.t: The inner linen curtains woven with cherubim
The goat-hair tent and the outer coverings
The veil and the placing of the furniture

doctrines.note: The veil divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place and makes visible a graded approach to God. Holiness is not only a quality but a boundary, and God himself decides where it runs.

The God whom heaven cannot contain chooses to be housed in a tent, plain outside and glorious within. His presence among his people is real, and it moves with them rather than waiting for them in one fixed place.
The veil keeps sinners from the presence of God, and only the high priest may pass it, once a year and with blood (Leviticus 16). The barrier and the appointed way through it belong together.

words.note: Paroket, the veil or curtain before the ark. The word is used almost only for this partition, the most solemn boundary in Israel's worship. It hid the ark from sight and shielded the priests who served in the Holy Place. The Gospels report that at Jesus' death “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38).

Keruv, cherub. In Scripture cherubim are heavenly beings who guard God's holiness and bear his throne: they guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24), and Ezekiel sees them beneath God's throne (Ezekiel 10). They are not the plump infants of later art but winged guardians, closer to the composite winged creatures that flanked thrones and palace gates in the ancient Near East.

Qeresh, frame or board, the upright unit of the tabernacle's walls. Whether these were solid planks or open, ladder-like frames through which the colored linen could be seen from inside is debated; solid boards of this size would have been very heavy to carry. Elsewhere the word names a ship's deck (Ezekiel 27:6), and its uncertain sense is one reason reconstructions differ.

christ: Hebrews reads this chapter's veil as a key to the work of Christ. The layout of the tent, with a first room for the priests and an inner room entered only by the high priest once a year, showed that “the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed” (Hebrews 9:8). Christ, the letter says, entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, and believers may now draw near “by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:20). Matthew and Mark record that when Jesus died, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38), which the church has read as a sign that access to God now stands open through his death. The tent as a whole stands behind John's statement that the Word “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14).

hard.q: Was the tabernacle real, or a later picture of Solomon's temple projected back into the wilderness?
hard.a: In the late nineteenth century Julius Wellhausen argued that the tabernacle of Exodus 25-40 was a historical fiction, the Jerusalem temple made portable and set back in the time of Moses by priestly writers in or after the exile. He pointed to the lavish materials, the fine craftsmanship expected of freed slaves in the desert, and older texts that describe a simpler tent of meeting pitched outside the camp (33:7-11). Many critical scholars still regard the priestly tabernacle as at least an idealized picture shaped by later temple practice. Others argue for an early core. They cite Egyptian parallels for portable gilded shrines and royal camp tents, features that differ from Solomon's temple rather than copy it (a tent rather than a stone house, goat hair and skins, acacia rather than cedar), and later references to a tent sanctuary before the temple existed, at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1) and in God's words to David, “I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling” (2 Samuel 7:6). The historical question remains open. The chapter's theological claim, that God chose to live among his people in a portable house of his own design, does not depend on settling it.

questions: From outside, the tabernacle looked like an ordinary goat-hair tent; its beauty was inside. What does that suggest about where God's glory is usually found?
The veil kept people back from God and also marked the place where the high priest would pass through. How do you experience God's holiness as both distance and invitation?
Every loop and clasp was there to make the tabernacle one whole. What small, unseen acts of faithfulness hold a community of faith together?
